`ResultsStrategyFactory` builds one `FixedQueuePool` in `__init__` (result_consumer.py:133) and hands that same instance to every strategy created in `create_thread_queue_parallel_worker` (result_consumer.py:254-259). Arroyo calls `create_with_partitions` again after each rebalance, and it closes the previous strategy first. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close()` and `terminate()` call `self.queue_pool.shutdown()` (lines 338, 342). That sets `worker.shutdown = True`, shuts every queue and ends the worker threads, and nothing recreates them. The factory still holds the dead pool, because `queue_pool` is only cleared in `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown`. The next strategy therefore runs on a dead pool. In `submit`, `work_queue.put()` raises `queue.ShutDown`. The broad `except Exception` at line 317 catches it, logs it, then calls `add_offset` and `complete_offset` for that offset (lines 320-325). The commit loop then treats the offset as done and commits it. From the first rebalance on, every message is silently dropped and its offset committed. The other modes do not have this problem: `create_thread_parallel_worker` also uses a factory-owned executor, but closing `BatchStep` or `RunTask` does not shut that executor down. The tests never create a second strategy after closing the first, so none of them catches this.

Fix: have the strategy own only its commit thread, and leave pool shutdown to `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown`. Or build the pool inside `create_with_partitions`. Also make `submit` leave the offset uncommitted when `put` fails, rather than marking it complete.

The shared `OffsetTracker` is also never cleared on rebalance. Offsets for revoked partitions stay in it, and the commit loop passes them to `commit` in the same dict as the partitions that are still assigned. If arroyo rejects offsets for unassigned partitions (I did not check its source), one stale partition would make the whole commit fail every second. Reset or prune the tracker per strategy.

Queues are unbounded, so there is no backpressure despite what the docstring says

The `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` docstring (line 253) promises "Natural backpressure when queues fill up". But every queue is `queue.Queue()` with no `maxsize` (line 185). `submit` never blocks and never raises `MessageRejected`, and `poll` only emits a gauge. Arroyo therefore keeps polling Kafka at full speed even when the workers are slower, for example during a DB slowdown. Queued `WorkItem`s, each holding the decoded result and the original message, grow without limit, which risks OOM. Offsets are only committed after processing, so a crash would replay everything. Either bound the queues and raise `arroyo.processing.strategies.abstract.MessageRejected` when the target queue is full, or drop the claim from the docstring and add a depth limit.

Commit stalls permanently on any non-contiguous offset

`get_committable_offsets` only advances across consecutive integers. The loop at lines 89-93 breaks at the first offset that is not in `all_offsets`. Kafka offsets are not always dense: log compaction and transaction markers leave gaps, and the consumer never sees those offsets. If a gap occurs, the committed offset stops there for good and `all_offsets` grows without bound, so the consumer is stuck without errors. `test_offset_gaps_block_commits` asserts this as the intended behaviour. The usual approach is to track offsets by submit order, not by integer adjacency. Commit up to the highest offset such that every offset submitted before it has completed, using a sorted or ordered structure of what was actually submitted.

Shutdown can block for about 100 seconds, and `join` repeats it

`FixedQueuePool.shutdown` joins each worker one after another with `timeout=5.0` (lines 242-243). Nothing makes the waits overlap, so with the default 20 workers all busy on slow DB work, the worst case is 20 × 5s. `close()` adds a 5s join of the commit thread first (line 337), for about 105s in total. `join(timeout)` ignores its argument and calls `close()` again (line 345), which can add another 100s. During a rebalance this blocks the consumer's poll loop for far longer than the usual Kafka `max.poll.interval.ms`, so the consumer may be kicked out of the group. Use a single shared deadline, for example `deadline = time.monotonic() + timeout` with `join(max(0, deadline - now))`, and honour the `timeout` argument in `join`. Also commit once more with the completed offsets on a clean close.

Commit function is called from a background thread

`_commit_loop` calls `commit_function`, which calls arroyo's `commit` callback (result_consumer.py:249-252), from a separate daemon thread while the main thread keeps polling and handling rebalance callbacks. Arroyo's commit callback normally runs on the processor thread, and I did not confirm that the Kafka consumer's staged-offset state is safe to use from two threads. Is this safe? If not, collect the committable offsets on the thread that calls `poll()` and commit there. That also removes the need for the 1s wake-up thread.

- `test_different_groups_distributed` (line 98) asserts that 20 string keys hit all 3 queues. `hash(str)` is randomised per process, so this fails by chance, about 0.1% of runs.

The commit thread ticks every second independently of the test. If a tick lands while only some items are complete, it commits a partial offset, sets the event, and the equality assertion fails. In `test_handles_invalid_messages` (line 327), a tick between the two submits commits only offset 100. Wait until the expected value shows up, or call `get_committable_offsets` directly.

`ResultProcessor.__call__` already starts its own `sentry_sdk.start_transaction` (result_consumer.py:48-51). The worker wraps every item in a second transaction (line 136), so each item produces two nested transactions. The `queue_depth` gauge is also emitted in `finally` for every processed item (line 150), which is a lot of metric traffic at uptime volumes. The `poll()` gauge already reports total depth. Consider emitting it on a timer or dropping it.

"Concurrent subscriptions" test never checks concurrency

The docstring says different subscriptions are processed concurrently. The test only asserts that the mocked processor was called twice, which a fully serial consumer would also satisfy. The grouping key is the subscription id (src/sentry/uptime/consumers/results_consumer.py:605-606) and the queue is `hash(key) % num_queues`. With `max_workers=2` the two random subscription ids land on the same queue about half the time, so concurrency is not guaranteed even by design. To test it, make each mocked call block on a `threading.Barrier(2)` with a timeout (this needs the two subscription ids to map to different queues). Otherwise rename the test to what it checks.

The only assertion is `factory.queue_pool is None`, which `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown` sets unconditionally (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/result_consumer.py:183-185). It does not show that queued items were drained. Patch `type(factory.result_processor).__call__` as the sibling tests do, and assert the call count is 5 after `shutdown()`.

Tests never close the strategy, so each leaks a commit thread

Every new test calls `factory.shutdown()` but never `consumer.close()`. `SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy` starts a daemon commit thread in `__init__` that loops until `shutdown_event` is set (src/sentry/remote_subscriptions/consumers/queue_consumer.py:268-291). `ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown` stops only the queue pool. All five results use the same subscription, so they always hit one FIFO queue and ordering is trivially preserved. A regression in the group-to-queue mapping would not be caught. Interleave results from a second subscription and assert per-subscription order. Also note that `send_result` builds every message with the same `Partition(Topic("test"), 1)` and offset 1, so these tests do not exercise offset tracking.

`if commits_made:` is always true after `assert commit_count >= 1` (both come from the same `tracked_commit`), so it silently makes the offset assertions optional only in a state the line above already rules out.
